ec512dfec1f5d2f6.subject: Douglas Murray: Europe’s Borderless Dream Becomes a Nightmare
ec512dfec1f5d2f6.body:

The images were unforgettable. More than 60,000 migrants entered the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta from Morocco over the course of 24 hours.
It’s arguably the most vivid illustration we’ve ever seen of the migrant crisis that has transformed the face of Europe in one decade and that continues to consume the continent’s politics. And no one saw it all coming more clearly than our own Douglas Murray. His 2017 book, The Strange Death of Europe [ https://substack.com/redirect/416226a0-c6fc-4951-9796-b5e87e08b0c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], chronicles the errors of judgment that led Western leaders so carelessly to open their doors to unlimited migration.
Will the brief storming of Ceuta prompt a reckoning among European elites, or will the crisis linger on, with the same denials and failed solutions from the leadership class? Read Douglas’s take on what comes next. —The Editors
Eleven years ago, almost to the day, Europe was experiencing a migration wave that threatened to make the continent buckle. In the space of a matter of weeks, more than a million people from Africa, the Middle East, and the Far East made their way into Europe, principally by crossing to the islands of Greece and Italy: “the soft underbelly of Europe.”
As various European countries started to panic, it was German chancellor Angela Merkel who decided to control the day. “Wir schaffen das,” she said in August 2015. “We can do this.” Merkel and some of her counterparts in the EU effectively suspended normal immigration procedures and opened the borders of Europe to anyone who wanted to come.
In those days, the route into Europe via Spain was relatively quiet. That was because the option of getting into Europe via Central and Southeastern Europe had been opened up, so there was less need for migrants to use the Spanish option. There were also effective agreements with the Moroccan authorities—unlike those in lawless Libya, for instance—which saved Spain from the most challenging of the 2015 waves.
Still, Spain remained uniquely vulnerable. Not least because, like Greece and Italy, the country had an accident of geography. This was the fact that, as well as being a remarkably short sail from North Africa, Spain has two territories actually in Northern Africa: the enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla...

L’Italie veut suspendre l’Espagne de l’espace Schengen
La cheffe du gouvernement italien d’extrême droite Giorgia Meloni veut suspendre l’Espagne de l’espace Schengen, après que des centaines de migrants sont arrivés illégalement dans l’enclave espagnole de Ceuta en provenance du Maroc.
“Nous sommes en train de réunir les instances compétentes et, à l’issue de ces réunions, nous sommes prêts à agir, y compris par des mesures exceptionnelles, comme la suspension de l’accord de Schengen avec l’Espagne”, a écrit la Première ministre, en dénonçant les “images choquantes” de Ceuta. “L’Italie ne restera pas les bras croisés”, a-t-elle affirmé.
Le vice-Premier ministre et chef de la diplomatie italienne Antonio Tajani s’était dit plus tôt “favorable à la fermeture de l’espace Schengen avec l’Espagne”. Matteo Salvini, également vice-Premier ministre italien et chef de la Ligue, a lui appelé à “suspendre Schengen” et “défendre les frontières” de l’Europe.
De son côté, le ministre des Affaires étrangères espagnol, José Luis Albares, a dénoncé la “démagogie”, et a convoqué l’ambassadeur italien en signe de protestation. Le message du ministre italien des Affaires étrangères Antonio Tajani “est inapproprié” de la part “d’un pays partenaire et ami dont nous attendons une solidarité européenne et non une démagogie partisane”, a-t-il déclaré sur le réseau social X.
Ceuta confrontée à l’arrivée de plus de 1 500 migrants en quelques jours
L’arrivée massive de personnes sur la côte de Ceuta par la digue de Tarajal met en évidence une nouvelle crise migratoire dans cette ville autonome espagnole. Il s’agit d’une répétition des scènes observées en mai 2021, lorsque des milliers de personnes avaient fait de même, submergeant les services d’urgence de la région.
Selon le président de Ceuta, Juan Jesus Vivas, le nombre d’arrivées a augmenté ces derniers jours. En moyenne, environ 300 personnes traversent depuis le Maroc à la nage ou à l’aide de dispositifs de flottaison. Il souligne également que le bilan des victimes de cette situation ne cesse de s’alourdir. Plus de 60 personnes ont déjà perdu la vie en mer.
La garde civile a été déployée le long de la frontière sud afin d’endiguer cet afflux de migrants. La délégation du gouvernement a déclaré que la gendarmerie marocaine coopérait. Cependant, des sources au sein de la garde civile de la ville affirment que cette aide est superficielle et ne parvient pas à endiguer la pression.
Face à cette situation, Juan Jesus Vivas a appelé le gouvernement à déclarer “l’état d’urgence national” et à prendre en charge la “gestion centralisée” de la pression migratoire, ainsi qu’à adopter des mesures visant à “faire face à la crise en mobilisant des ressources et à prendre en charge la charge financière que cela représente pour la ville”.
Le gouvernement a déjà répondu à la demande du président de Ceuta, écartant la possibilité d’une déclaration d’état d’urgence national. “La déclaration d’état d’urgence national relève de la réglementation de l’Etat en matière de protection civile, qui ne considère pas les flux migratoires comme un risque dans le cadre du Système national de protection civile et ne prévoit pas non plus de plans spécifiques”, ont déclaré des sources du ministère de l’Intérieur.

L’UEFA menace de boycotter les Coupes du monde
Face à la volonté de la Fifa et de son président Gianni Infantino de créer une filiale commerciale ouverte à des investisseurs privés, les fédérations membres de l'UEFA ont annoncé qu'elles “ne participeront pas aux compétitions de la Fifa” si ces propositions voyaient le jour, “à moins que celles-ci ne soient abandonnées dans leur intégralité et que des garanties fermes ne soient données quant au fait que la Fifa n’ouvrira plus jamais sa gouvernance ou ses compétitions à la propriété privée”.
“Dès l’instant où des investisseurs extérieurs acquièrent des participations dans les compétitions de la Fifa, le football change à jamais”, poursuit l'UEFA. “À partir de ce moment-là, chaque décision concernant le calendrier international, chaque décision relative aux formats des compétitions et chaque décision façonnant l’avenir du football n’est plus guidée par ce qui sert au mieux le jeu, mais par ce qui sert au mieux les actionnaires. Ce modèle n’a pas sa place dans le football mondial. L’avenir du football ne peut être dicté par les attentes de ceux dont le premier devoir est de maximiser le rendement financier.”
L’instance mondiale a donné aux fédérations nationales de football jusqu’au 19 septembre pour se prononcer sur la proposition, qui doit obtenir une majorité pour être approuvée, promettant un versement de 20 millions d’euros supplémentaires à chaque nation qui y consentirait.
“Il est à la fois irresponsable et indéfendable qu’une proposition d’une telle importance pour le football ait été élaborée en secret et amenée au bord de l’adoption sans aucune consultation significative avec ceux à qui il incombe de veiller sur ce sport. Les fédérations nationales du monde entier se voient désormais confrontées à un ultimatum : accepter la mainmise irréversible sur les plus grandes compétitions de football ou en subir les conséquences. Il ne s’agit pas d’une décision démocratique, mais d’une gouvernance par l’intimidation, un acte de coercition indigne d’une institution chargée de la gestion du football mondial”, estime l’UEFA.
Plus tôt dans la journée, la World Leagues Association, qui regroupe 47 ligues professionnelles issues de cinq confédérations continentales différentes, avait déjà publié un communiqué dans lequel elle “demande à la Fifa de retirer son projet et réaffirme la nécessité d’un changement fondamental dans les processus décisionnels de la Fifa”. 
Plainte de Rima Hassan contre le journaliste Jean Quatremer
La députée européenne de La France insoumise, Rima Hassan, a déposé une plainte au parquet de Paris contre le journaliste Jean Quatremer, pour harcèlement en ligne. 
En cause, une série de messages postés par Jean Quatremer, depuis son profil sur le réseau social X, pendant un an. “Rima Hassan y a été mentionnée à 157 reprises en l’espace d’un an, faisant d’elle la quatrième personnalité la plus citée sur ce compte”, expose la plainte. Ainsi, entre le 1er juin 2025 et le 31 mai dernier, le journaliste “a fait usage ou relayé les appellations ‘Rima Hamas’ et ‘Lady Gaza’ respectivement à 18 et 9 reprises”. “L’ensemble de ces publications cumule plus d’un million cinq cent mille vues sur la plateforme”, est-il écrit dans la plainte, qui dénonce “un acharnement” et “une campagne de harcèlement en ligne à laquelle ont également participé de nombreux autres utilisateurs du réseau social X”.
À ces “désignations répétées” s’ajoutent plusieurs publications portant des accusations. 1d7412decdc2f08a.subject: The Chaos in Ceuta and Another European Migrant Crisis. Plus. . .
1d7412decdc2f08a.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.thefp.com/p/the-chaos-in-ceuta-and-another-european-migrant-crisis-plus

It’s Friday, July 31. This is The Front Page, your daily window into the world of The Free Press—and our take on the world at large. Today: The meaning of the Salman Rushdie verdict. Should you skip your annual physical? How Markwayne Mullin drew the ire of President Donald Trump on July 4. Is Ukraine turning the tables on Russia? And much more.
But first: The chaos in Ceuta.
Sixty thousand. That’s how many people local authorities estimate have crossed from Morocco into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta over the past 24 hours. It is, by any measure, an extraordinary figure, coming close to the territory’s total permanent population of nearly 84,000. Also extraordinary: the footage of the crossings. Droves of mostly young men jumping out of trucks at the border, swimming around breakwaters, clambering over fences, sprinting down streets. At least 18 people have died during the chaos, and the Spanish government has deployed the army to Ceuta.
The scenes recall the peak of Europe’s migrant crisis a decade ago—and underscore how little Europe’s elites have done to address the problem in the intervening years. Rod Dreher recently returned to the U.S. from living in Europe, where he watched as political leaders repeatedly refused to tackle the issue, and Europeans only grew angrier. In our pages today, he reacts to the dystopian scenes from Ceuta, and asks: What will it take to break the immigration taboo? —The Editors
EDITORS’ PICKS
All across the country, Americans are angry about data centers. They’re too big, they say, too noisy, and too costly for the communities that have seen their electric and water bills rise. But data centers are also inevitable, and absolutely essential in the coming age of AI. Joe Nocera lays out a “peace plan” that will allow for the continued build-out of data centers while mollifying the concerns of local communities. It includes transparency, improved construction technology—and plenty of money.
In early July, when Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said that women shouldn’t have to play sports against biological males, America more or less shrugged. When, a week later, reporters gave her the opportunity to walk back her remarks, she doubled down: “I said what I said. I think it’s kind of common sense.” This, says columnist Kat Rosenfield, is a sign of progress. Not so long ago, there would have been howls of outrage and attempts to cancel Cunningham. What has brought on this sea change? Kat’s thesis: “Americans of all political stripes are sick and tired of pretending they can’t see the emperor’s whole entire ass.” Who can doubt it?
For years, Laura Loomer, the MAGA influencer, sided with Russia in its war against Ukraine, even contributing articles to Russia’s state-run network, RT. But after visiting Ukraine, and meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky and other top officials, she concluded she had been on the wrong side. On Tuesday, from her hotel room in Ukraine, she spoke to Eli Lake about her change of heart, and tells him she now considers Zelensky “an essential ally.” Notes Eli: “By the looks of things, so does the president.”
When Alex Berenson’s 81-year-old mother got a tax bill for $55,048 she was baffled. She had lived in her New York City townhouse for 30 years—and she knew she didn’t owe that kind of money to the city. The answer, it turns out, was Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s new “pied-à-terre” tax, which is designed to dun out-of-towners who own fancy New York apartments but whose primary residence is elsewhere. The incident leads Alex to muse on everything from inept city bureaucracy to Mamdani’s socialism, to the heartlessness of social media. “Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax isn’t just about pied-à-terres,” he writes. “It’s about stoking resentment toward an ever-expanding list of class enemies.”
Every six months, Tanya Lukyanova spends a few weeks in Moscow, where she was raised and where she still has friends and family. Since 2022, when the war against Ukraine began, she never saw the effects of the war in Russia’s capital, as the government sought to keep it insulated. But this visit was different. Tanya reports that she saw long lines of people waiting for their ration of gas, heard people talking about seeing drones and hearing explosions, and discovered a bitterness about the war that she hadn’t experienced in earlier trips. “Nobody can explain what we’re fighting for,” said one man after a few drinks. “Why do people die every day? To what end?”

Hello and welcome back! This week has brought us many special funny treasures, and I’ll be honest, they’re mostly concerning a man called Anthony Fauci. Buckle up, buttercups.
→ HRH Fauci!: Anthony Fauci, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, kept a journal. A diary filled with love notes to himself. Which I’ve literally never heard of a man doing, but that’s beside the point. I guess he also did it on his work computer [ https://substack.com/redirect/52582823-8c10-4cba-bd58-d99ed41bf457?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], because Senator Rand Paul obtained and released it [ https://substack.com/redirect/3b503015-4a76-4633-b6d3-db0a640f2260?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. I’m not sure where to begin. First, let’s get a sense of the tone. He carefully documents all the glitzy celebrations of himself, lists all the [ https://substack.com/redirect/ecf8e857-adf0-445a-a89b-e3a1930397ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] “movie stars and athletes” he has a Zoom call with, and carefully logs [ https://substack.com/redirect/09381529-2068-44e8-9880-27d7f61243ce?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] all the celebratory news stories about himself. It’s like an Excel spreadsheet of compliments. For a sense, here’s Anthony Fauci on Anthony Fauci [ https://substack.com/redirect/12dd3d9c-6dc1-49e9-99a8-78dcb77b708f?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]:
Big front page article abut me appeared in the Washington Post. Very flattering. The situation with my national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable. It is not hyoperbole to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable peson in the world. (Countless profiles on me in multiple media. I cannot even read all the things that are written abuyt me since I am so busy . . . seriously. POTUS seems to be enamored of me even though I am taking the spotlight away from him. We are developing a very unique and interesting relationship. The entire secret service corps is coming over to me and chatting. They let me into the first gate without even checking ID. Everyone is worried about my health and welfare, probably because it is all over the place that I am almost 80 years old.
He loved being a celebrity. The thing about it is, he really was being worshipped! There was a cult of Fauci. People were getting Fauci tattoos and dancing with images [ https://substack.com/redirect/e546c5d8-8573-4ca0-9872-8c2653c77bac?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] of Fauci. He really was on the cover of every magazine, which, if you think about it, was weird! If millions of Americans suddenly made me their cult leader, and I had previously just been an unknown short man in the back of an HIV press conference, I would go insane with power too. So would you. And when you see lockdowns in the context of a power-drunk elf getting turned on by the idea of canceling Easter—he’s typing so fast he can barely keep up—you can understand better what we all lived through. For him, the pleasure was canceling things, especially things he felt gave power to the right (sports, family gatherings, religious events). We can never forget the freaks who gain power in a centrally controlled system. Also: no diaries, ever, certainly none in Google Docs. I write my grocery lists on Signal, and you should too. Love letters via email have been forbidden until further notice. I will be dragged up in front of Congress one of these days, but so help me God, they aren’t going to know about one brunch I attended. Next up, the lab leak:
→ No one ever thought it was the wet market: In his diaries, Anthony Fauci clearly thought a lab leak was possible or even probable. Even as the whole elite intelligentsia made belief in wet-market origin a litmus test for being a good person for God knows what reason. Here’s Anthony Fauci in his journal [ https://substack.com/redirect/9284f5c5-cb10-4199-b901-bfaac99f21ff?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] in 2020:
It now appears using epi data and genomic data that the first infection was in early December and was not connected to the market. The infections spread among people weeks before the Chinese reported that they were dealing with a new infection and that gave the virus time to establish itself in multigenerational (sustained) spread. Remember, early on the Chinese were saying that there is no human-to-human transmission and all the original 27 cases were from the market. Now we know the market was not the source, it was the amplifier. Having said that, somewhere the virus jumped from animals to humans.
And Fauci himself thought it could definitely be tied to the gain-of-function research [ https://substack.com/redirect/cff9dcba-16ff-498d-a62c-6b136f84687d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] he knew was happening with Covid viruses in Wuhan. GOF is gain of function, which is basically when scientists give a virus a new trait (or “function”) so they can see how it behaves. Again, here’s Anthony Fauci:
There was not total agreement about the likelihood of deliberate insertion. Ron Fouchier said he was sure that this could occur naturally and we should not waste our time and divert effort to pursue this. This is expected of him since he was the original GOF person with Yoshihiro Kawaoka. Also, Christian Drosten was with Ron; the rest felt that deliberate insertion was possible, and given the fact that Dr. Shi Zhengli at the University of Wuhan has been working for years in GOF in coronaviruses to allow adaptation of the spike protein to bind to the human ACE2 receptor, we could not let this go.
To remind everyone: Suggesting that the U.S. funded gain-of-function research on Covid in Wuhan was considered slightly insane at the time. But in 2016 there was literally a Wuhan-linked coronavirus researcher writing [ https://substack.com/redirect/15b2e602-f6a6-4cdc-97f9-ed3d8a2be5f9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]: “This is terrific! We are very happy to hear that our gain-of-function research funding pause has been lifted.” The only reason I knew about any of this earlier was by reading a lunatic blog called ZeroHedge, that was like, Hey, there’s a Covid-making lab in Wuhan. In 2021, The New York Times’ global health reporter posted [ https://substack.com/redirect/a49358cf-a9c5-45aa-a612-74d1d0c7a9e4?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]: “Someday we will stop talking about the lab leak theory and maybe admit its racist roots. But alas, that day is not yet here.” Racism is the cudgel that will hit you if you question why we have to wear a hazmat suit to walk to the mailbox. (She apologized amid [ https://substack.com/redirect/22c3e5aa-145d-402d-ae34-fddf1fda71a7?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] backlash.) Never mind how it’s maybe more racist to say the Chinese gave us this disease from weird animals they eat and not from a sophisticated laboratory? Anyway, here’s NPR [ https://substack.com/redirect/b21bd339-1680-436d-b3a1-d4bb33479442?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], again after Fauci’s own writing that gain-of-function research in Wuhan was a possible source of the virus:
Oh, also? Fauci knew in February 2020 that Covid’s case fatality rate was pretty low [ https://substack.com/redirect/e8327b63-ba77-4f28-8b51-945eda85ffc0?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. He wrote, “This is acting like a bad influenza in its transmissibility,” and that the fatality rate is “more like 0.2-0.3 percent rather than 2.0 percent.”

57c92eeba2478840.body:
View this post on the web at https://linguasinica.substack.com/p/taiwan-conquest-film-shelved

Scheduled for release over the past weekend, the Chinese action war film The Belief (澎湖海戰), a dramatic depiction of the 1683 Qing conquest of Taiwan, seemed on track to define a new and, for many, concerning genre — the “forced-unification blockbuster.” But the film, it appears, has run aground, its planned debut coming and going in silence.
Produced by a consortium of investors with a reported budget of 500 million yuan (about 70 million dollars), and backed by the state-owned Changchun Film Studio [ https://substack.com/redirect/d3c716de-9447-4d8a-8c2d-1d48a3055475?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], The Belief centers on the 1683 naval battle at Penghu, an island 50 kilometers from the main island of present-day Taiwan, a country official policy in Beijing insists [ https://substack.com/redirect/a64f97e5-0a49-4a5d-8cbb-43491237bfd2?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] has been “an inalienable part of Chinese territory since ancient times.” The setting is the outset of the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), as Qing forces seek to defeat remnants of the Ming dynasty (1368-1644) holding out in Taiwan.
The allegorical connection to present-day tensions, which have resulted in persistent military exercises in the strait [ https://substack.com/redirect/1915ea1f-cd48-4bff-904e-9e1034fa188a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and containment of Taiwan internationally [ https://substack.com/redirect/07184b40-f324-4b1d-8e0f-fad8d1146fff?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], is so plain it scarcely needs mentioning. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) regards the island as unresolved business from a civil war fought in the 1940s with the Kuomintang [ https://substack.com/redirect/56930b9e-a96f-443f-a12a-061cea169512?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], now one of several political parties in a democratic Taiwan.
The Belief has been heavily promoted by state media [ https://substack.com/redirect/40645b41-a85f-4d70-b00a-d4109928f082?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], including the CCP’s People’s Daily, since its first trailer dropped on October 25, 2025, the 80th anniversary of Taiwan’s “retrocession” from Japanese colonial rule at the end of World War II. An announcement on May 22 said it would be released on July 25. But the film, with its swashbuckling scenes of battles at sea, has so far not set sail — leading to speculation about what calculations China might be making.
And this is reportedly not the first delay the film has faced. According to BBC Chinese [ https://substack.com/redirect/19dcbc27-4fec-4955-9080-f869a99534de?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], it was already pulled from a planned Lunar New Year release back in February — prior to the May reschedule giving it the summer release date that passed on Saturday.
Media outside China have noted over the past week that the film’s official Weibo [ https://substack.com/redirect/3828fd36-0f2c-4cae-ae68-82f42aba2e9d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] account has not been updated since June, and that the film remains unavailable on China’s domestic movie-ticketing website [ https://substack.com/redirect/9b71f0f1-4489-4a19-a655-02e258d54a22?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
The film has stimulated heated discussion in the media in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and beyond. The Taipei Times noted in an editorial [ https://substack.com/redirect/97586634-a74c-4e1f-9a57-e77e75ed4d2c?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] that the film’s tagline, “the unification of Taiwan is an unstoppable trend,” was lifted straight from a speech by Chinese President Xi Jinping.  [ https://substack.com/redirect/1b39e698-df9d-4f63-b1a4-e100b55aa10e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]Storm Media [ https://substack.com/redirect/1b39e698-df9d-4f63-b1a4-e100b55aa10e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] quoted Liu Hsing-jen (劉性仁), an associate professor at Chinese Culture University’s Institute for National Development and Cross-Strait Studies, warning that the film’s marketing — casting a historical civil war as a clash of “us or them” — could send the international community the wrong signal that China was preparing for war, undercutting Beijing’s actual strategy of favoring “peaceful unification” while applying gray-zone pressure.
Taiwan outlets ETtoday [ https://substack.com/redirect/0a74840a-e346-4169-9f97-dd7c1b10184a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and Newtalk [ https://substack.com/redirect/097a582d-7135-438f-add7-30b3b6480299?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] both cited Fan Shih-ping (范世平), a professor of East Asian studies [ https://substack.com/redirect/6f0c1ced-faa2-40b7-b9fd-8fb26d87d0b3?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] at National Taiwan Normal University, as saying the film has likely courted controversy on several fronts. First, it risks being read by audiences as an implicit rebuke of China’s leadership for not acting on its strong rhetoric about the “reunification” of Taiwan, in contrast to the conquering Shi Lang.
Further, it glosses over an inconvenient historical fact, according to Newtalk’s account of Fan’s analysis. Shi Lang’s attack on Taiwan was essentially a military conquest, not something the Taiwanese people actively welcomed, said the professor. If history is romanticized this way, he argued, the international community may more readily conclude that a Chinese military invasion of Taiwan would likewise constitute an act of aggression — seriously damaging Beijing’s international image.
Perhaps adding to the trouble, Shi Lang, the film’s protagonist, is a historically fraught choice of hero.
Media in Taiwan have generally referred to The Belief as a “force-unification blockbuster” (武統大片), giving the invasion scenario it depicts exactly that sense of unwantedness. “And that’s not really unfair,” Hong Kong’s HK01 [ https://substack.com/redirect/9c07d088-b560-473e-bac4-d21ba37cc9fd?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] noted in a related report.
Perhaps adding to the trouble, Shi Lang, the film’s protagonist, is a historically fraught choice of hero. He originally served Zheng Chenggong (鄭成功), the Ming loyalist commander, before defecting to the Qing and leading the campaign to crush Zheng’s successors. This betrayal, as Newtalk [ https://substack.com/redirect/097a582d-7135-438f-add7-30b3b6480299?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and others have reported, has made him the target of online accusations that he was in fact a “Han traitor” (漢奸).
Understandably, the film has also sparked lively debate online among so-called “Han nationalists,” also known as Huang Han [ https://substack.com/redirect/4d3d176b-912e-417b-ad2e-53f07b9e3e8e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (皇漢). These nationalists subscribe to a narrative called the “1644 historic perspective” (1644史觀), whose intellectual roots trace back [ https://substack.com/redirect/19dcbc27-4fec-4955-9080-f869a99534de?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] to the Republic of China era (1912-1949), when some scholars attributed China’s modern-day weakness and humiliation entirely to Qing rule, casting the Manchus, the ethnic group that founded the dynasty, as colonizers. A related trend of “Ming fans” (明粉) emerged in China about twenty years ago, driven by the runaway popularity of a bestselling history book Those Things in Ming Dynasty [ https://substack.com/redirect/c89e30b9-bb35-45fd-

This week, we’re cherishing Jimothy, translating The Odyssey, and getting advice from 10-year-olds.
SELF-DISCOVERY
Great expectations
Emily North explores the experience of “having potential,” and the weight that comes with ambition.
now what am i going to do with all this potential?
—emily north  in angel cake [ https://substack.com/redirect/fa002b2e-660f-405e-94e2-167eb8bdb880?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
i do not have a fear of aging, but instead i have a fear of time passing and me not opening my mouth wide enough to catch everything. some of you may know one of my favorite quotes is, “kiss the joy as it flies” but lately i don’t just want to kiss it, i want to stick my tongue so far down its throat before it has to leave. i have dedicated this summer to being the one where i do literally whatever i want at all times. as a rule this is how i like to live my life 365 days a year but this summer in particular i have been practicing joie de vivre as if it was a prayer and i am on my knees begging for nothing about my life to change i promise to be good i promise i will be fun and sexy and kind forever i promise i promise i promise i will do anything thank you God amen.
walking around with the weight of your potential has a special kind of power to make you notice the pace at which days, weeks, years fly by in your calendar. i spent the past week with my extended family where my tiny cousins have somehow morphed from toddlers into little teenagers who are able to do k-pop choreography with precision, i overheard my little brother taking work calls from the dining room using a low voice i have never heard before, my sister was talking about when she wants to have a baby, and i realized my parents have had the beach house for almost ten years. lately time has been moving as slow as honey, except for when it slides down my throat it burns instead of feeling sweet. i feel i am wasting my time by lying in the sun and reading books and drinking too many martinis and staying out way too late on a weeknight… i could be using this time to become a better daughter, sister, colleague, friend, future partner and instead i am lying in a pool of my own sweat, physically and emotionally drowning in myself. my anxiety about the slipping of time is extremely self-indulgent, so much so that even typing this essay has made me lose my appetite. to be so obsessed with the pace of your own life and its potential blinds you from the people you pass along the way. happiness fuels self-obsession, despair fuels self-obsession, all i want to do is feel numb and forget who i am and never face anyone who thinks about my potential ever again.
at my best, when i chug along the rosy pink path i make for myself i know that my potential is not finite, it has no expiration date, and i am a girl of exceptional tenacity to make her life exactly how she wants; however, i would be lying if i said i didn’t crack from time to time and think about when it will all eventually leave me.
Keep reading [ https://substack.com/redirect/6128b2b1-619c-439d-b83b-4beee1ffb597?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
PERSPECTIVE
HUMANITIES
“I hate to be that guy, but the book is a lot better than the film”
Emily Wilson, a classical scholar who has translated both The Odyssey and The Iliad, shares her thoughts on Christopher Nolan’s adaptation in an excerpted Q&A.
If you can bear to hear the truth you’ve spoken/twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools... [ https://substack.com/redirect/44ce1a41-6ca1-4dbf-b167-d35788ac01cf?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
—EMILY WILSON  in EMILY’s Substack [ https://substack.com/redirect/9360e86e-042d-4542-a7d5-24223a2740ca?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
You’ve dedicated much of your career to bringing the Odyssey to life. What are your initial reactions to the film?
I very much hope many people go and see it in cinemas—it’s worth it to see it on the big screen, because so much of the movie is about the visual effects, as well as the very loud soundtrack. This film is an event, and it has a lot of memorable moments. But I hope those who do so will also read or reread the poem. I hate to be that guy, but the book is a lot better than the film.
You’re the first woman to have her translation of the Odyssey published in English. What does that mean to you, and why does it matter?
Mostly, I don’t think it matters at all. It’s a silly little factoid, not something particularly relevant for my actual work. Gender wasn’t a topic in my scholarly or critical work before I began work on the Odyssey. I’d published various books and articles, mostly about male authors and male characters, with very little attention to gender. I’d published earlier translations—of Seneca’s tragedies—and none of the reviewers or readers of those translations seem to have thought my gender mattered for that work, and nor did I. But all of a sudden, “Woman Translates Odyssey” became the universal headline, and then journalists began to ask me endlessly and unstoppably about my supposedly female or feminine or feminist perspective. Whatever I say or do, it continues even unto this day.
I’ve found it quite limiting to have my work constantly framed by journalists in terms of my gender. I see it as both simplistic and anti-feminist to insist that all women’s work has to be viewed as primarily “women’s”, as if all our toys must be pink and no other color—whereas men, lucky things, get to focus on what they actually care about, which might not be gender at all. Everything a woman does has to be described as a “feminist intervention”, even if she doesn’t see it in those terms at all (which I certainly don’t). As members of the unmarked gender category, men get to imagine that their gender has nothing to do with their interpretations or perspectives on the world or on literature or history. I keep urging journalists to ask men about their gender and how it informs their work, and please stop asking me about it, because I really don’t work on gender and it’s not my main interest... but those pleas don’t seem to be going anywhere.
I took on the project of re-translating the Odyssey, and then the Iliad, for reasons that had nothing to do with my gender identity, but had to do with my specific scholarly training and literary sensibilities, as someone with longstanding interests in poetic and narrative form, the long traditions of both ancient and early modern verse, and a very long-standing interest in drama and dramatic narrative. I felt that there was an opportunity to provide English readers with translations in traditional, regular meter—in contrast with the dozens of existing free verse and prose translations—and versions that would, like the originals, have a supple multiplicity of voice and perspective, as well as their emotional directness and vividness. Those proto-dramatic qualities are flattened in many existing translations. In approaching any dialogue or scene in the Homeric poems, I make a conscious attempt to understand how the text portrays multiple perspectives, and I don’t assume ahead of time that women characters will be presented as inferior or ridiculous. But that’s surely not feminism; it’s about being a reasonably responsible, competent translator of these great poems. The bar for what “feminist translation” means ought to be a lot higher than that.
Beyond my own specific work: the fact that most translations of ancient texts into English have been done by men is notable and quite surprising. There are plenty of English-speaking classicists of all genders, so it’s not about lack of people who could do it, in theory. Plenty of women scholars have written books and articles about Homer. The scenes in Ceuta on Thursday were extraordinary.
Over the course of just a few hours, some 50,000 people crossed from Morocco into the small Spanish territory on the North African coast - many swimming around the frontier barriers, others forcing their way through the land border. The arrivals were equivalent to roughly 70 per cent of Ceuta’s normal population.
According to press reports, at least 57 people died, while the Spanish government deployed soldiers and thousands of police officers to restore control.
Government officials said that the surge was the result of trafficking networks that exploited confusion surrounding a recent Supreme Court judgement restricting the immediate return of migrants intercepted at sea: rumours swirled that anyone reaching Ceuta would be allowed to remain, drawing thousands towards the frontier.
The scenes of the border crossing being overwhelmed went viral. They prompted Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez to describe the events as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity.
Italy suspended the Schengen free movement regime with Spain on Friday, temporarily closing land and sea borders, with Italian FM Antonio Tajani calling this a ‘necessary measure to safeguard the security of our citizens.’
And of course, the video scenes went viral around the world, fuelling anti-migration narratives and - predictably - vast amounts of chatter about Europe being overrun by migrants, foreigners and Africans; gold dust, in other words, for far-right political parties.
Why, though, did so many people cross at once? 
In this post, I am going to try to explain...

Welcome back to The Weekend Press! Today, Suzy Weiss drinks with pro-pied-à-terre-tax socialite Julie Macklowe, whose politics have made her the skunk at Hamptons garden parties. Spencer Klavan remembers a fallen Irish folk hero. River Page on living in a secular sharia state. And more!
But first: Frannie Block meets the 25-year-old who’s saving local news.
My first job out of college was working the night shift as a cops and crime reporter at The Des Moines Register. I’d sit at my desk listening intently to the police scanner, and hop in my car as soon as I heard a whiff of action and drive straight to the scene. I loved this paper and still do—the people I worked with are among the most dedicated, smart, and kind colleagues someone could ask for.
But while I was there, I knew I was watching a business model failing in real time. In six months, I had survived two rounds of layoffs, watched the boss who hired me take a voluntary buyout to save our jobs, and found out I was getting furloughed for a week over Christmas. My new editor managed more than a dozen writers on his own after the shrinkage.
With fewer and fewer reporters, our owners, Gannett—the largest newspaper chain in the country—told us to shift our focus from long, in-depth investigations to shorter stories with catchier headlines to try to boost our online presence. At weekly staff meetings, we’d brace ourselves for the latest signs of a business in free fall.
By the time I left, I’d seen a Pulitzer Prize–winning paper once lauded for its biting political coverage depleted into a shell of its former self.
The state of local media in America today brings me great sadness, but when I heard about Evan Newton in Monticello, Georgia, I felt a twinge of hope.
Newton is 25 years old, and two weeks ago, he emptied his savings to purchase his local newspaper from its longtime owner to save it from being bought by a conglomerate or shutting down altogether. Young and ambitious, Newton told me he couldn’t just “sit on the sidelines” and watch the paper he grew up reading wither away. So I hopped in the car again and drove to the office he’s now running—to meet someone brave enough to identify a problem in his community and take a risk to fix it.
“I’ve never owned a business,” said Newton cheerfully, who admitted he barely graduated from college. And yet, he’s got a plan. . . —Frannie Block
Second Thought
The journalist Amy Chozick specializes in women who spike the blood pressure of the body politic. Hillary Clinton. Lauren Sánchez Bezos. The Kardashian sisters. She’s profiled them all—and in this week’s episode of Second Thought, she talks about their messy realities with Suzy Weiss. They also chat about Amy’s brand-new book, With Friends Like You—which is about what happens when a girlboss becomes a mom.
“Our generation of women was raised on, ‘You can do whatever a guy does,’ ” Amy says, “I don’t think men were raised to be like, ‘You can do whatever a woman does. You can load the dishwasher and cook every night and do the grocery shopping.’  ”
Watch their conversation below, or listen wherever you get your podcasts. And to read Suzy’s reflections on their chat, don’t miss her newsletter [ https://substack.com/redirect/24706f0b-6256-456b-803d-094e71a4155b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]!
​​Knock Knock, It’s Cupid!
A new batch of ads from single Free Pressers is live on the site. Click here [ https://substack.com/redirect/67dea85f-e13f-4e80-8440-1ef8b890ea60?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] to meet a student of Brazilian Zouk dancing; a Philly sports fanatic; or a shih tzu mom “partial to a dirty martini with a rare steak.” Your special someone could be just one email away! If you’d like to take a chance at Free Press love, write a paragraph that defines you, including your age, where you live, and what you’re looking for, and send it over to Cupid@TheFP.com [ https://substack.com/redirect/497a2b2e-905b-4f83-a521-b3778be42de3?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
This week, Kat Rosenfield wrote about Sophie Cunningham—the college basketballer who said “young girls in sport shouldn’t have to go against biological men,” and didn’t get canceled. Arthur Brooks reflected on the tragedy of looksmaxxing. And River Page complained that the internet forces us to live in a secular sharia state. . .
How should you spend the rest of your weekend? We asked our reporter River Page for his recommendations…
📺 Watch… The New World. Although hated by many audiences and critics upon its release, Terrence Malick’s 2005 take on the Pocahontas story is perhaps the greatest movie about America ever made. Malick doesn’t whitewash conflict between the settlers and natives, but he doesn’t spend a great deal of time moralizing about it either. His main interest is the pure strangeness and curiosity of two completely different societies with no previous knowledge of each other meeting for the first time—a phenomenon nobody in the globalized world will ever truly experience again.
📚Read… A Feast of Snakes [ https://substack.com/redirect/4534accb-1e2d-4324-82df-87364ebe7ab9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], by Harry Crews. It’s one of the few novels that documents the transition from the old South to the new. Set in the small town of Mystic, Georgia, it follows Joe Lon Mackey—a former football star turned alcoholic wifebeater—as he prepares for the town’s annual Rattlesnake Roundup, a festival wherein locals hunt, kill, and eat the town’s snake population. This book has everything: castration, crazy agoraphobic women, adultery, dogfighting, and, of course, murder. And it’s a quick read.
💰Buy… Things on eBay. Almost nothing is made well anymore—from particleboard furniture, to cheap clothes, to AI-slop wall art—but thankfully, whatever it is you’re looking for, no matter how niche, there is a boomer in Wisconsin with a hoarding problem who has a version of it that’s stood the test of time in their garage, and who now wants to sell. Half the decor in my house and a decent portion of my clothes have come from these heroes—and none of it has immediately broken or fallen apart in the way that Amazon trash will. So the next time you want to redecorate, or want to find a vintage wool sweater for $15 (like I did last winter), log on and enjoy the journey. (Author’s note: Ebay isn’t paying me to say any of this, but it should!)
Last but not least: When we asked our creative director Clara Grusq for the most beautiful thing she’d seen this week, she told us that she just rewatched the late ’90s classic, The Talented Mr. Ripley—and she couldn’t get enough of this sun-soaked Mediterranean shot.
That’s all, folks! Have a great weekend.

4cf8e6c46a3841d6.subject: 🟨🟧 Des drones comme en Ukraine contre les tueurs d’élèves
4cf8e6c46a3841d6.body:
View this post on the web at https://philippecorbe.substack.com/p/des-drones-comme-en-ukraine-contre

Hi everyone, c’est Zeitgeist, depuis New York.
Je vais vous raconter l’histoire du “Nostradamus de l’IA”. Le petit génie a bâti un empire de 45 milliards de dollars… qui a failli s’effondrer totalement au moment où les invités arrivaient pour son mariage.
Une saga familiale qui déchire deux élus trumpistes. Pourquoi un sénateur a-t-il attendu deux ans avant de dénoncer son ancien gendre, accusé de violences par sa propre fille ? Elle affirme même qu’il a braqué une arme sur sa tête pendant qu’elle changeait leur bébé. Deux ans ? Est-ce parce qu’il craignait de fâcher Trump ? Ou parce qu’il avait peur que son ancien gendre confirme des rumeurs d’homosexualité ?
Et Spider-Man qui frôle le record du plus gros démarrage de l’histoire du box-office en Amérique du Nord. Jamais Hollywood n’avait engrangé autant de recettes en un weekend.
Du pur Trump.
Et les Iraniens ont bien compris son petit jeu.
Vendredi, il annonçait sur un ton martial que les forces américaines allaient “les frapper très durement”.
Samedi, elles étaient, selon lui, “prêtes à faire feu”.
Et dans la nuit, il y a renoncé, avant d’aller jouer au golf dimanche matin et de gagner le tournoi qu’il organisait sur son propre parcours de Bedminster, dans le New Jersey.
Pour la quarantième fois, s’est-il vanté.
“Cela s’appelle le TALENT. Moi, j’en ai, eux non ! 
Président DONALD J. TRUMP.”
Dans le vol retour pour Washington, le président explique que “l’Arabie saoudite, les Émirats arabes unis, le Qatar et l’Iran le lui ont demandé”.
L’appel téléphonique du prince saoudien MbS a compté.
Il vante aussi, a posteriori, l’ampleur de l’attaque qui n’a donc pas eu lieu.
“Nous avions préparé une attaque qui aurait été la plus importante depuis la SECONDE GUERRE MONDIALE.
Elle aurait été DÉSASTREUSE POUR EUX.”
Il annonce que des discussions avec Téhéran commencent aujourd’hui et pourraient aboutir à la réouverture du détroit d’Ormuz, route commerciale stratégique, ainsi qu’à “un accord sur le nucléaire”.
Le prix du baril baisse. La journée devrait être agréable pour les investisseurs qui avaient parié qu’il ne mettrait pas ses menaces à exécution.
J’ai l’impression de vous avoir chanté cette rengaine à plusieurs reprises depuis cinq mois. Trump menace d’une escalade, puis annonce l’imminence d’un compromis.
Alors, pour une fois, laissez-moi commencer ce matin par autre chose que par Trump.
J’ai découvert il y a quelques jours, dans un reportage de la matinale de ABC, qu’il y aura, à la rentrée, dans quelques écoles, des drones déployés pour empêcher (ou plutôt abréger) les fusillades.
Quand j’étais correspondant ici, j’ai l’impression d’avoir vécu la même scène je ne sais combien de fois. 
Breaking News à la télévision. Des images d’hélicoptères des chaînes locales. L’annonce que des élèves d’une école, d’un lycée ou d’une université sont confinés. Alerte au tireur. Les forces de police arrivent. Des enfants et des adolescents fuient en courant. Ils hurlent, pleurent. Ils ne savent pas encore lesquels de leurs camarades sont tombés. Parfois, ils connaissent même le tireur. C’est souvent l’un des leurs.
Maintenant, imaginez la même scène avec des drones capables de briser des vitres, d’aveugler le tireur avec des lumières, de l’asperger de spray au poivre ou de le percuter à près de 100 kilomètres-heure.
Ce sera en place dès la rentrée.
Je vous raconte. 
Ça peut sembler fou, mais c’est le nouveau dispositif qui va être installé dans plusieurs écoles américaines. Au moins neuf établissements de Floride, de Géorgie et du Colorado dès cette rentrée.
Ce n’est pas une dystopie, mais la nouvelle ligne de défense contre les fusillades dans les écoles.
Le projet a été conçu par Mithril Defense, une entreprise d’Austin, au Texas, qui l’a baptisé Campus Guardian Angel, l’ange gardien des campus.
Elle s’est inspirée directement de la manière dont les forces ukrainiennes utilisent de petits drones sur le champ de bataille. Le fabricant assure que l’objectif n’est pas de tuer, mais de distraire, de désorienter et de neutraliser un tireur jusqu’à l’arrivée des forces de l’ordre.
Les appareils en plastique sont entreposés dans des boîtiers sécurisés à l’intérieur des écoles.
L’alerte pourra être donnée par un bouton d’urgence placé dans une salle de classe ou par une application.
Une fois la menace confirmée, des pilotes professionnels prendront les commandes à distance depuis le siège de l’entreprise au Texas. Même si c’est à des milliers de kilomètres de l’établissement.
Selon Mithril Defense, ces drones peuvent parcourir les couloirs à plus de 80 km/h et retrouver l’assaillant en moins de 15 secondes. Comment pourront-ils le reconnaître ? Grâce à des caméras. Ils seront aussi équipés de sirènes et de puissantes lumières. Un haut-parleur diffusera la voix des opérateurs à distance. Le drone permettra aussi de guider les policiers vers le suspect ou de leur montrer ce qui se trouve derrière une porte. Ils pourront même passer par certaines fenêtres grâce à une pointe fixée à l’avant.
Et ce n’est pas un drone, mais plusieurs drones qui entreront en action. Ils pourront d’abord encercler le tireur, faire retentir leurs sirènes, pour alerter les autres élèves, et produire de fortes détonations.
Ils pourront projeter un produit chimique au poivre qui empêcherait le tireur d’avancer.
Et si ce n’est pas suffisant, ils pourront même percuter un tireur en fonçant sur lui à près de 100 km/h.
Le cofondateur de Mithril Defense est un ancien des troupes d’élite des Navy SEALs :
“Une fois que les drones sont sur vous, vous ne pouvez tout simplement plus leur échapper.”
Tout ceci reste encore en phase d’expérimentation. Les appareils ont été testés lors de simulations, mais jamais encore au cours d’une vraie fusillade.
Ce projet est né après le massacre d’Uvalde, au Texas, en mai 2022. Un homme armé avait tué 19 enfants et deux enseignantes dans une école primaire, tandis que des policiers attendaient pendant plus d’une heure avant de pénétrer dans la salle de classe.
C’est au cœur de l’argumentaire de l’entreprise. Les premières minutes d’une attaque sont les plus meurtrières et un drone peut pénétrer dans une pièce sans risquer la vie d’un policier. Si l’appareil est abattu, il suffit d’en envoyer un autre.
La Floride finance une expérimentation dans trois lycées publics. La Géorgie, dans cinq. Dans le Colorado, une école publique qui accueille des élèves de la maternelle à la terminale a prévu de financer son dispositif avec des fonds privés.
Pour un établissement, l’abonnement coûterait environ 20 000 dollars par an, selon Mithril Defense. Ça peut sembler cher, mais les écoles américaines dépensent déjà quelque quatre milliards de dollars chaque année pour renforcer leur sécurité avec des caméras, des détecteurs d’armes, comme dans les aéroports, et d’autres technologies.
Évidemment, tout cela pose de nombreuses questions. Que se passe-t-il si un enfant est atteint par le produit irritant ? Et si l’opérateur à distance confond, dans la précipitation, un élève en fuite avec le tireur ?
Des familles de victimes trouvent que ces appareils interviennent trop tard. Ils ne surgissent qu’une fois l’attaque commencée. Est-ce donc à cela qu’il faut consacrer des fonds ?
J’ai lu à cette occasion dans le Washington Post un chiffre impressionnant. Depuis la tuerie de Columbine en 1999, qui avait inspiré un grand film de Gus Van Sant et un documentaire marquant de Michael Moore, près de 400 000 élèves ont été exposés à la violence par arme à feu dans une école américaine.
🟨🟧 Le “Nostradamus de l’IA”, ou la chute d’un empire
Connaissez-vous le “Nostradamus de l’IA” ? 
C’est le surnom donné à Leopold Aschenbrenner. Il n’a que 24 ans, mais en deux ans, son fonds, Situational Awareness, a bâti un portefeuille de 45 milliards de dollars. Il a su convaincre les investisseurs que l’intelligence

Caption: 

Hey there,

Rowan here, founder of The Rundown.

Back in March, we surveyed hundreds of thousands of you with one question: how can we make The Rundown better?

One answer came back louder than everything else. Thousands of you asked us to expand the Community AI Workflow section -- that small feature at the bottom of every newsletter that highlights one reader's real AI workflow each day.

This honestly surprised me. We already share AI workflows every single day, and if anything, I assumed we'd been sharing too many.

So I dug in a little more. I took calls with readers, sent emails, and read through thousands of survey responses. A clear pattern came up:

1. My assumption _was_ correct that readers don’t want more “AI workflows“ from execs, influencers, the media, or hype chasers.

2. But readers DO want more AI workflows from _real_ people doing _real_ work with AI. The everyday knowledge workers, the builders, and the AI curious.

Then it clicked. Over 2 million of you read this newsletter, and every day we get workflows we don't have room to feature. You didn't need us to find these people -- you needed a place to find _each other._

So we built one.

[The Community AI Workflow Hub](https://app.therundown.ai/community) is our new one-stop shop to learn how everyday builders are actually applying AI -- and to share your own.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/b6224af4-a4a4-4a2b-b78b-489864122c5f/Screenshot_2026-08-01_at_9.16.17_AM.png?t=1785600993)
Follow image link: (https://app.therundown.ai/community)
Caption: Screenshot from the Community AI Workflow Hub

It's purposely simple. Unlike other communities, we intentionally launched it without a maze of channels, chats, buttons, or features to get lost in. Browse by what you're trying to solve, copy the prompts and steps, and put them to work on the same day.

To top it off, every day we're featuring the top submission in the newsletter -- in front of 2M+ readers -- with a link to the reader's LinkedIn. Something core to me is making sure readers win with us as we grow. So each day, one of you gets put in front of the founders, operators, and hiring managers who read The Rundown. Build something cool, share it, and we'll promote you.

(Fair warning: this might fill your DMs -- questions about the build, recruiters, job offers.)

[Sharing takes 5 simple steps](https://app.therundown.ai/community?submit=open), and we use a little AI on the backend to format your post for you, so it can be raw and unfiltered.

The rules are straightforward:

* Share workflows you actually run -- a rough-but-real setup beats a polished concept

* Show the how, not just the wow: include the tools, steps, and prompts 

* No spam or drive-by promotion (we have community moderators on staff 24/7)

Tom Verrilli is the chief product officer at Whatnot, a live shopping platform that’s become the fastest-growing U.S. marketplace business in history, with over $8 billion in GMV. Before joining Whatnot, Tom was CPO at Twitch and director of product growth at Twitter (during one of the most turbulent periods in the company’s history).

1deda60ea8b738e6.subject: La Chine accélère dans l’IA avec un modèle hors norme
1deda60ea8b738e6.body:
View this post on the web at https://foudelatech.substack.com/p/la-chine-accelere-dans-lia-avec-un

Grâce à NotebookLM, l’IA générative de Google, chaque édition se transforme aussi en court échange audio : un format condensé, vivant et facile à écouter.
🎧 Écouter l’épisode audio de cette semaine
1. Moonshot AI: la société chinoise qui pourrait bouleverser la domination mondiale de l’IA avec Kimi K3
La course mondiale à l’intelligence artificielle compte un nouveau concurrent de taille. La jeune entreprise chinoise Moonshot AI, soutenue notamment par Alibaba et Tencent, a présenté Kimi K3, un modèle multimodal à poids ouverts conçu pour programmer, analyser de vastes ensembles d’informations et mener des projets complexes. Avec 2 800 milliards de paramètres, il représente le plus grand modèle ouvert annoncé à ce jour. Son arrivée confirme surtout que les acteurs chinois ne se limitent plus au marché local : ils cherchent désormais à rivaliser avec OpenAI, Anthropic, Google et DeepSeek sur les outils les plus avancés.
Un modèle géant pensé pour les tâches professionnelles
Kimi K3 repose sur une architecture dite « mixture of experts », qui n’active qu’une partie de ses 896 groupes spécialisés pour chaque demande. Cette approche permet théoriquement d’augmenter les capacités du modèle sans multiplier les ressources de calcul dans les mêmes proportions. Moonshot met également de l’avant une fenêtre contextuelle d’un million de jetons, suffisante pour analyser de très longs documents, d’importantes bases de code ou plusieurs centaines de pages dans une même conversation.
L’entreprise vise particulièrement les développeurs avec Kimi Code, un agent capable de lire et modifier des fichiers, d’exécuter des commandes dans un terminal et de corriger son travail après avoir détecté une erreur. Accessible notamment dans Visual Studio Code, il pourrait aussi répartir certaines étapes d’un projet entre plusieurs sous-agents : recherche, programmation, vérification ou création de présentation. L’entreprise chinoise prévoit publier les poids du modèle le 27 juillet 2026, une étape qui permettra aux chercheurs et aux entreprises de l’évaluer plus concrètement.
Des promesses ambitieuses, mais plusieurs questions ouvertes
Moonshot affirme que Kimi K3 atteint des résultats comparables aux meilleurs modèles fermés dans la programmation, le raisonnement et l’utilisation d’outils logiciels. Des évaluations indépendantes initiales semblent positives, particulièrement pour le code et les tâches agentiques. Elles ne placent toutefois pas clairement Kimi K3 devant les systèmes les plus puissants d’OpenAI et d’Anthropic. Les comparaisons présentées par l’entreprise doivent donc être interprétées avec prudence tant que davantage de tests indépendants demeurent inaccessibles.
Son prix pourrait néanmoins attirer les organisations : Moonshot annonce environ 3 $ US par million de jetons en entrée et 15 $ US en sortie, avec des rabais importants pour les données conservées en mémoire cache. Cette stratégie peut séduire les entreprises qui réutilisent de longs documents ou de grandes bases de code. Cependant, un modèle de cette taille restera difficile à héberger localement et dépendra souvent de l’infrastructure infonuagique de la société chinoise ou de fournisseurs spécialisés.
Enfin, « à poids ouverts » ne signifie pas nécessairement « open source ». Les données d’entraînement, les méthodes de constitution du corpus et les conditions exactes d’utilisation restent inconnues. Sa fiabilité, sa sécurité et les éventuelles restrictions de contenu devront aussi être examinées de près.
Finalement, Kimi K3 ne constitue pas encore une victoire définitive sur les géants américains, mais son lancement envoie un signal fort. Moonshot AI combine un modèle massif, des fonctions agentiques avancées et une tarification agressive pour s’imposer auprès des développeurs. Les évaluations après la publication des poids détermineront si Kimi K3 devient une véritable alternative mondiale ou simplement une nouvelle démonstration de la progression rapide de la Chine dans l’IA avancée.
2. Samsung mise sur l’IA et les appareils pliables au Galaxy Unpacked 2026
Samsung profite du Galaxy Unpacked du 22 juillet 2026 pour franchir une nouvelle étape dans sa stratégie mobile en présentant les Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Z Fold8 et Z Flip8, ainsi que les Galaxy Watch Ultra2 et Watch9. Au-delà des caractéristiques techniques, le fabricant sud-coréen veut démontrer que les appareils pliables ont suffisamment évolué pour répondre à des usages variés, de la productivité à la création de contenu. Samsung ne cherche donc plus seulement à impressionner avec un écran qui se replie : sa stratégie consiste à relier ses téléphones, ses montres et Galaxy AI dans un même écosystème, à un moment où la concurrence dans le haut de gamme s’intensifie.
Le Fold8 Ultra devient la vitrine de la productivité mobile
Le Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra incarne l’offre la plus ambitieuse de Samsung. Il adopte un écran intérieur de 8 pouces, une luminosité maximale annoncée de 3 000 nits, un capteur principal de 200 mégapixels et une batterie de 5 000 mAh. Avec ses 215 grammes et son épaisseur de 4,1 millimètres une fois ouvert, Samsung cherche à rapprocher son pliable d’une tablette compacte, sans sacrifier la mobilité.
Le Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 propulse l’appareil, qui peut afficher jusqu’à trois applications simultanément. Il prend aussi en charge Samsung DeX, qui permet de le relier à un écran, un clavier et une souris. Le Fold8 Ultra vise ainsi les personnes qui travaillent sur des documents, participent à des vidéoconférences ou créent du contenu depuis leur téléphone.
Le Galaxy Z Fold8, plus léger avec ses 201 grammes, privilégie quant à lui un format plus compact et un écran intérieur de 7,6 pouces. De son côté, le Galaxy Z Flip8 conserve son format à clapet, mais privilégie les interactions rapides du quotidien. Avec un poids de 180 grammes et une épaisseur de 6,1 millimètres une fois ouvert, il se veut à la fois compact et facile à transporter. Son écran externe permet de consulter des informations sans déplier l’appareil, notamment les rendez-vous, les rappels, la météo, les actualités et d’autres données personnalisées grâce à Now Brief. Samsung cherche ainsi à transformer cet écran en véritable tableau de bord personnel, afin de réduire le nombre d’actions nécessaires pour accéder aux informations essentielles.
Galaxy AI et les montres renforcent l’écosystème Samsung
L’intelligence artificielle occupe une place plus importante dans cette génération. La fonction Now Nudge peut, par exemple, proposer d’ajouter un événement au calendrier après la réception d’une invitation. Cette approche proactive peut simplifier certaines tâches, mais elle soulève aussi une question essentielle : quelles données personnelles doivent être analysées pour que ces suggestions soient pertinentes ?
Samsung met de l’avant Knox, Knox Vault, le traitement local de certaines données et un tableau de bord consacré aux actions de l’IA. Ces protections s’avèreront importantes, car l’entreprise souhaite analyser davantage de signaux provenant des messages, courriels, calendriers, notifications et habitudes d’utilisation.
Les Galaxy Watch Ultra2 et Watch9 complètent cette stratégie. La première vise les sportifs avec un boîtier en titane, une batterie de 800 mAh et des outils liés à la course, à l’hydratation et à la plongée. La Watch9 se veut plus légère et adaptée au suivi quotidien du sommeil, de l’activité et de la récupération. Ces fonctions demeurent toutefois des outils de bien-être : elles ne remplacent pas un avis médical.
Avec les Fold8, Flip8 et les nouvelles Galaxy Watch, Samsung consolide son avance dans les appareils pliables. Dear Free Presser,
In case you missed them, we had a number of must-read stories last month that covered the full spectrum of Free Press journalism—illuminating essays on modern life, forays into our current DSA-dominated political moment, high-stakes investigations, and, of course, a hefty dose of Tough Love.
Here they are—for paid subscribers only. Unlock full access and you’ll also get the Forum [ https://substack.com/redirect/3df2a4b7-fb96-49b8-b534-0fdb21c99982?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], Supper Clubs [ https://substack.com/redirect/ee26f2e2-2ff4-4972-bb01-e91802133a67?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], free gift subscriptions, and more.
Frannie Block wrote one of the most devastating stories [ https://substack.com/redirect/3bd95a06-d63e-4455-a0d2-c3ac39db160c?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] we’ve run all year: A New York school suspended a 15-year-old boy over a sexual assault allegation, never called his parents, and never let him defend himself. He died by suicide hours later.
On the political front, Jake Altman spent over a decade inside the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and walked through what the organization’s new platform reveals [ https://substack.com/redirect/fff10c9a-fa6d-4bf1-a970-62aa7f625da4?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] about what its rising stars actually believe. Evan Barker, a former Democratic operative who worked alongside many of those same candidates, argued that this is only the beginning [ https://substack.com/redirect/0019f3bc-aa3d-44ad-81b8-872744800a97?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] of the party’s leftward lurch.
Meanwhile, Douglas Murray dug into why New York mayor Zohran Mamdani is turning a local mayoralty into a proxy war [ https://substack.com/redirect/17abb363-b1bc-4494-8725-79ee3dc390f4?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] with Benjamin Netanyahu. And in one of our most-discussed essays of the summer, Niall Ferguson teamed up with AI researcher John-Clark Levin to make a chilling case: The tools that once beat back Holocaust denial are losing to AI and the algorithm [ https://substack.com/redirect/f2d22121-34a3-4e3f-ad41-75def4162b4e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
Tanya Lukyanova reported the story of a young man who went into the ICU and died without a doctor ever physically examining him [ https://substack.com/redirect/12e1110b-65b1-4d9b-9fbe-14cab12a1ae7?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]—treated instead by a physician on a screen, 12 miles away.
Finally, Abigail Shrier told a 39-year-old man [ https://substack.com/redirect/624e5b0f-bac9-4934-9b90-bc71cce241ce?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] exactly why his “overall wonderful partner” leaves him drained after every date. And Arthur Brooks was refreshingly honest about the contradiction at the center of his own life—a happiness expert who can’t stop running himself into the ground [ https://substack.com/redirect/2ab2b2b2-56f0-4283-ae31-6e1e4d570192?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
All of it is waiting for you. To access these stories and support honest, fearless journalism, become a paid subscriber.
With gratitude,

38b8b0eb02bd2b8a.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.thefp.com/cp/209673247

“You’re getting killed in the comments!” It’s not a text any writer wants to receive, but I wasn’t surprised. After all, I’d just written a piece [ https://substack.com/redirect/45bed606-f917-4d21-858b-6fce22f645ad?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] that was gently critical of America, and Free Press readers are a patriotic bunch; of course you leapt to your country’s defense.
For context: I’m British, I’d just been in an active-shooter situation in Washington, D.C., and I was reflecting on the Second Amendment. “Is it worth it letting civilians have guns? Does it really make this country more free?” I wrote. “Can you explain it to me? I want to know.”
I meant what I said. I genuinely wanted to hear from someone who believes what half the American population believe [ https://substack.com/redirect/0a47b46b-f6ae-4ca7-b5bf-42da522595f5?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]s: That it’s important to protect a citizen’s right to bear arms. The whole point—and the privilege—of being a journalist is getting into the hearts and minds of people who think differently.
Which brings me back to that text I got—the one about being killed in the comments.
It was from my friend and colleague Larissa Phillips, who I’ve edited since she joined The Free Press two years ago—and who happened to be perfectly placed to answer my appeal: “Help me understand.” Because once upon a time, Larissa herself was vehemently anti-gun—and now, she’s planning to get one.
A thread that runs through a lot of Larissa’s writing [ https://substack.com/redirect/01860965-f0da-40a9-b58d-a117653166fb?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] here at The Free Press is how moving from bright-blue Brooklyn to a red area of upstate New York changed her perspective—on Republicans [ https://substack.com/redirect/f6e4d83e-b81e-47f0-a1c8-4326ea9e7831?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], on marriage [ https://substack.com/redirect/2afa964f-66a1-435c-85fe-352d893368f9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], on America itself [ https://substack.com/redirect/280fa4fc-27dd-4f17-a799-f026b2e76113?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. In today’s essay, she writes that when she left New York City, she wouldn’t even let her kids have a water gun, but moving to a part of the country where firearms are a part of daily life, she slowly came to question her assumptions about the Americans who owned and used them.
This is the story of how she fired a bullet for the first time.  —Freya Sanders
I jammed my palm right up against the grip, wrapped fingers around my firing hand, extended both arms, and squinted at the target through my glasses. With all systems in place, there was nothing left to do but pull the trigger. Bam! At a velocity of about 800 mph, the bullet shot down the barrel of the gun in my hand and seemed to instantaneously punch through the target. I checked my handiwork. A tiny hole had appeared just a couple inches south of the white circle in the middle. Not bad for my first time ever firing a pistol. I looked at my instructor. “Can I go again?”
Until very recently, I could not have imagined taking lessons on how to shoot a handgun. I have spent most of my life extremely opposed to every single type of firearm. Guns are involved in most murders; they escalate volatile situations, land hotheaded young men in prison, and kill innocent people. I grew up the child of two anti-war idealists who deplored violence, and as a suburban kid, I had little exposure to hunting, which I imagined as a pastime for drunk slobs who wanted to massacre wildlife. When I grew up and became a parent myself, I was haunted by the specter of school shootings. The Columbine High School massacre in Colorado happened just two weeks after my first child was born in 1999; I held my tiny infant against me as I took in the horror on the news.
Not long after that, I set down roots in Park Slope, Brooklyn, where the default position on guns was: They’re bad; let’s get rid of them. We wondered: What if we stopped making them? Can we hold gun manufacturers liable for gunshot deaths? What about a buy-back program like Australia did? I readily participated in these conversations, even though I was not as extreme as some of my friends, who said things like: “No guns. Ever.” I thought some people should have guns, but only highly trained, background-checked professionals. At the time, I didn’t know anyone who had a gun—and the prospect of owning one myself never crossed my mind.
But since moving from one of the most liberal places in the country to a farm in a red part of upstate New York, my views on firearms have shifted dramatically. In fact, I’m actually thinking about getting a handgun...

ChatGPT Codex Voice + browser + Sites: an expert’s AI workflow | Nick Baumann (OpenAI)
Listen now on YouTube [ https://substack.com/redirect/02c141e4-574b-4443-b133-3c61315d7426?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] • Spotify [ https://substack.com/redirect/79213b21-3ea9-4ee4-9cff-6b14b940debf?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] • Apple Podcasts [ https://substack.com/redirect/b35bb6a8-e701-430a-afa7-2c22ed4c747d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Brought to you by:
Bolt.new [ https://substack.com/redirect/dc208b60-3193-465b-88c4-f1ee702f2079?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]—Turn your idea into a real product
Hyperagent [ https://substack.com/redirect/7e3c34ac-07b8-4a59-a2ed-d894544efa5d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]—Deploy fleets of agents that handle real work
Nick Baumann from OpenAI joins Claire to demonstrate how he uses ChatGPT, Codex, and Voice to automate huge parts of his work and life. He walks through advanced workflows for managing tasks in parallel, monitoring email and expenses, booking travel, building and publishing websites, and even turning dozens of raw clips into finished videos.
Biggest takeaways:
ChatGPT Codex Voice doesn’t just answer questions. It can actually operate your computer while you keep talking. Nick Baumann demos the new interface live: he triggers it with a hotkey, the orb reads what’s on his screen through Appshots, and Codex spins up separate threads to book a flight, file an expense report, and check his calendar at the same time. 
One of Codex’s most powerful features is also one of its least understood: thread-forking. When a task gets complicated, Codex can open a new thread, branch from an existing one, or pull context from previous conversations on its own. Users don’t have to manually organize everything first.
Heartbeats in ChatGPT Work offer a practical glimpse of always-on agents. Nick gets notified when a suspicious charge appears, a package is nearby, or an email needs his attention—and he set it all up without writing code.
ChatGPT Sites looks much closer to a real deployment platform than a lightweight demo. It includes a SQL database, file storage, environment variables, and email-based access controls. During the episode, Claire and Nick build and publish a live How I AI tips site, organized by tool and job function, in roughly the time it would normally take to set up a CMS template. For internal tools, small apps, and private resources, that starts to feel genuinely useful.
Nick’s video-editing workflow is one of the clearest examples of AI cutting real production work. He records 50 or 60 raw clips, uploads them, talks through the rough story he wants, and lets a custom plugin transcribe everything, scan the footage, choose the strongest takes, and assemble finished vertical videos overnight. What would normally eat up most of a content team’s day is largely handled while he sleeps.
Voice may be the best way to give AI context because it removes the pressure of figuring out exactly what to type. Claire calls this the “yapper’s API,” and the idea is simple: people often get more useful results when they talk freely than when they stare at an empty prompt box trying to be precise. Across two-person voice chat, mobile dictation, and Codex’s orb interface, the same pattern keeps showing up—people who talk to AI tend to give it more context, and more context usually leads to better work.
As AI gets more capable, latency is becoming a much bigger product decision. Nick often uses the highest-intelligence mode in Voice, but once a model has the tools it needs, speed can matter more than another small jump in reasoning quality. A lot of AI products are still designed around the assumption that waiting is unavoidable. As that changes, the tools that feel immediate will have a major advantage—especially for users who currently find AI too slow to bring into a live workflow.
